author: claire-harmon
title: 3 a.m. Anxiety in Perimenopause: Why It Isn't in Your Head
dek: What may be behind 3 a.m. anxiety in perimenopause, when to talk to a doctor, and a 10-minute tense-and-release practice to do in bed.
seo_title: 3 a.m. Anxiety in Perimenopause: Why It Isn't in Your Head
seo_description: 3 a.m. anxiety in perimenopause: what may be going on, when to talk to a doctor, and a 10-minute muscle relaxation practice to do in bed.
pull_quote: Your nights may have more to do with shifting hormones than with how well you cope.
body_html:
It's 3 a.m. Your heart is hammering. You're lying in the dark, running through every possible reason: the 2 p.m. coffee, the odd email from your boss, something you said to your sister three weeks ago.

You are exhausted. Your mind will not stop.

By morning you've reached the usual verdict: something is wrong with me. Maybe you've even been told it's stress, and that you should try to worry less. (Helpful.)

3 a.m. anxiety in perimenopause is something many women describe. No blog post can tell you what is causing yours. What this one can do is lay out what researchers have looked at so far, and give you one complete thing to do in bed tonight.

What may be going on with 3 a.m. anxiety in perimenopause

In perimenopause, estrogen doesn't decline in a tidy straight line. One endocrinologist describes estradiol in these years as erratic and, on average, higher than before, with progesterone running lower (Prior, 2002). Think less of a slow fade and more of a dimmer switch operated by a toddler.

Progesterone matters for a reason most women never hear. Your body turns some of it into a compound called allopregnanolone. A research review describes allopregnanolone as strengthening the effect of GABA, a chemical messenger that quiets nerve activity (Barth et al., 2015). Whether lower progesterone means less of that quieting for you, on a given night, is more than the review can tell either of us.

Then there is how the body meets stress. In a small pilot study, 15 perimenopausal women were followed for 12 weeks. The women whose estrogen marker fluctuated more had a higher heart rate during a lab stress test and reported more rejection, anger and sadness. The fluctuation was not linked to their cortisol or blood pressure (Gordon et al., 2019). That is a very small group, and a lab is a long way from your bedroom.

Sleep changes too. A 2018 review of sleep in the menopause transition tied sleep trouble to menopausal stage and hormone changes beyond age alone, and named hot flashes as a major contributor, many of them linked to awakenings (Baker et al., 2018).

Put together, these are findings about groups of women, and they can't say what is happening in your body. They do offer a kinder reading of a bad night. Your nights may have more to do with shifting hormones than with how well you cope.

Your nights may have more to do with shifting hormones than with how well you cope.

When to talk to a doctor

New or worsening palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, or anxiety that is getting in the way of your daily life are reasons to talk to a doctor. Sudden or severe chest pain is a reason to call for emergency help. Hormones are one possible explanation among several, and a doctor is the person who can sort through them with you. The practice below is meant to support professional care, and it does not replace it.

What to do in bed at 3 a.m.: tense and release

The practice is called progressive muscle relaxation. You tense one muscle group for 5 seconds, let it go completely, and move on to the next. It needs no light, no phone and no getting out of bed.

It has been tested in women near this stage of life. In a 2024 randomized trial, 63 postmenopausal women with poor sleep quality took part. Those who practiced it every day for eight weeks improved in sleep quality and fatigue (Sucu & Çitil, 2024). Two caveats: those women were past menopause, and the trial did not measure anxiety. So take this as something that may help your body settle. It comes with no promise of sleep.

Safety note: if you have an injury, recent surgery or chronic pain in any muscle group, skip that group and move to the next. Tension should be firm but never painful. If something hurts, release immediately.

Lie on your back with your arms at your sides. The workbook sets aside about 10 minutes for the full round, which leaves you room to move slowly. After each of the 8 muscle groups, rest for about 10 seconds before the next one.

  1. Hands and forearms. Squeeze both fists tightly. Hold for 5 seconds. Release completely, and feel the warmth and heaviness in your hands.
  2. Upper arms. Bend your elbows and flex your biceps, like a slow bicep curl. Hold for 5 seconds. Release, and let your arms drop heavy.
  3. Shoulders. Lift both shoulders up toward your ears. Hold for 5 seconds. Release, and let them drop as far as they go.
  4. Face and jaw. Scrunch your entire face: eyes, nose, jaw, forehead. Hold for 5 seconds. Release, and notice the muscles around your eyes and jaw softening.
  5. Neck. Press the back of your head gently into the pillow. Hold for 5 seconds. Release. Do not strain, and skip this step if you feel any sharp sensation.
  6. Chest and upper back. Take a deep breath in and hold it while you press your shoulder blades together. Hold for 5 seconds. Exhale and release.
  7. Abdomen. Draw your belly in toward your spine. Hold for 5 seconds. Release completely, and let your belly go soft.
  8. Legs and feet. Flex both feet, point your toes upward, and tighten your thighs and calves at the same time. Hold for 5 seconds. Release, and let your legs sink into the mattress.

To close, lie quietly for 60 seconds and breathe normally. Scan slowly from your feet to your face and notice what's different.

If 10 minutes sounds impossible while you're this wound up, do three groups only: hands, shoulders and face.

Tense and release is the last of four tools in Chapter 3 of the Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook. What the book adds to this page: three faster tools for the moments that can't wait ten minutes, and a planner where you choose, in daylight, which one will be your 3 a.m. tool.

What you might notice

Heaviness in your hands, your legs or your whole body. Warmth in a muscle just after you let it go. A sigh, a few tears or even a laugh, which is a strange thing to produce in a dark bedroom and is fine. You might fall asleep before step 8, which is allowed.

You might also notice nothing. That's common the first few times, and it doesn't mean you did it wrong.

If tensing leaves you more keyed up, or a muscle cramps, stop and breathe normally. Try the three-group version another night, or set this practice aside.

When to use it

  • At 3 a.m., when you're awake with a racing heart and a body that won't let go. Reach for your fists before you reach for your phone.
  • In the hour before bed, after a day of building tension.
  • In the morning, when you need a reset before the day starts.

This is a slow tool. When anxiety arrives fast and you want something that takes a minute or two, the physiological sigh is a better fit. And if you'd like a breathing practice for bedtime itself, Maya Chen's evening extended exhale is a gentle place to start.

And if broken nights are followed by foggy days, a notebook can show whether the two travel together: here is how to map menopause brain fog over 14 days.

A daytime follow-up: start your own record

The middle of the night is a poor time for analysis. In daylight, with a notebook, try these questions.

  • When did you first notice this anxiety, or notice it getting worse? A rough age or year is fine.
  • Does it follow any pattern in your cycle, or does it seem random?
  • What does it feel like in your body, before any thought shows up?

There's no right answer. You're drawing the first lines of a map, and it gives you something concrete to bring to your next doctor's visit.

Questions women ask about 3 a.m. anxiety in perimenopause

Why do I wake up at 3 a.m. with anxiety in perimenopause? No blog post can tell you what is causing yours. Researchers have looked at estrogen that swings while progesterone runs lower, at how the body meets stress, and at hot flashes that come with awakenings. Those are findings about groups of women, and hormones are one possible explanation among several.

Is a racing heart at 3 a.m. a perimenopause symptom? Many women in perimenopause describe it, and it still isn't something to assume. New or worsening palpitations, chest pain or shortness of breath are reasons to talk to a doctor, and sudden or severe chest pain is a reason to call for emergency help.

What can I do when I wake up anxious at 3 a.m.? One option is progressive muscle relaxation, done lying in bed: tense one muscle group for 5 seconds, let it go, and move to the next. It may help your body settle, and it comes with no promise of sleep. If the full round is too much, do hands, shoulders and face only.

These questions and the muscle relaxation practice both come from my book, The Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook, which has the seated version and three other calming tools. For tonight, two fists and a count of five are enough to begin.

author: claire-harmon
title: The Physiological Sigh: A Breathing Exercise to Calm Down in Perimenopause
dek: A breathing exercise to calm down when perimenopause puts your body on alert in a meeting, in the car or at 3 a.m.: two breaths in, one long breath out.
seo_title: The Physiological Sigh: A Breathing Exercise to Calm Down
seo_description: The physiological sigh, step by step: a breathing exercise to calm down in perimenopause, with counts, a safety note and what you might notice.
pull_quote: Regulation is often quiet at first.
body_html:
It's 2:47 on a Wednesday afternoon and you're in a meeting. Nothing dramatic is happening. Your chest tightens anyway, your thoughts speed up, and you're suddenly sure you're about to cry, leave, or say something you'll regret.

Most breathing exercises to calm down assume a quiet room and ten spare minutes. You have a conference table and a racing heart. The physiological sigh is a breathing exercise to calm down that fits inside the meeting itself. A round or two takes about 30 seconds, and nobody around you needs to know.

Many women in perimenopause describe this: a body that goes on alert for no obvious reason, in the afternoon meeting, at a red light, at 3 a.m. Arguing with the feeling rarely gets far. A breath gives you something physical to do while it passes.

What the physiological sigh is

Two breaths in through your nose, the second a small sniff stacked on top of the first, then one long, slow breath out. That's all of it.

Your body already does a version of this without asking you. Sighs happen on their own every few minutes to re-inflate the tiny air sacs in your lungs (Li et al., 2016). The practice borrows that pattern and does it on purpose.

The workbook sums up the tool in one line: "The exhale is where the calm lives." The second sniff fills your lungs a little more, which leaves room for a longer breath out. Your heart rate tends to rise after you breathe in and fall after you breathe out (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014). Whether that fully explains why a long breath out can feel settling is still an open question, so take the line as a description of how the practice feels to many women.

Why this breathing exercise to calm down may help

The pattern was tested in a small randomized trial from Stanford (Balban et al., 2023). For a month, 108 people, most of them students in an undergraduate psychology class, spent five minutes a day on one of three breathing exercises or on mindfulness meditation. One of the breathing exercises was cyclic sighing, which is this sigh repeated.

Every group felt less anxious after a session, and on anxiety there was no clear winner between the breathing and the meditation. The sighing group had a bigger lift in positive mood than the meditators and a bigger drop in breathing rate. The authors describe the study as exploratory.

Two limits are worth saying out loud. Those people practiced for five minutes a day, and the version below is far shorter. And they were mostly students, so the trial says nothing specific about perimenopause. What follows is something to try, with no promise attached.

Before you start

Safety note: if you have asthma, COPD or any condition that affects your breathing, check with your doctor before changing your breathing pattern. If you tend to hyperventilate or get light-headed easily, go slowly and keep the breath out shorter at first. Feel dizzy? Go back to normal breathing. If paying attention to your breath makes the anxiety louder, stop, open your eyes and look around the room. Naming three things you can see is enough. You can return to normal breathing at any point.

New or worsening palpitations, chest pain or shortness of breath are a reason to talk to a doctor, however sure you are that it's hormones. This practice is meant to support professional care. It does not replace it.

How to do the physiological sigh, step by step

Sit or stand comfortably. Eyes open is fine. The counts come from the workbook and move at about one per second.

  1. Breathe in through your nose, a full, normal breath. (Count to 3.)
  2. Sniff in a little more through your nose, without breathing out first. (About one second. Your lungs will feel full.)
  3. Open your mouth slightly and let one long, slow breath out, until the air is gone. (Count to 6 to 8. Longer than feels natural.)
  4. Pause at the bottom of the breath for 1 or 2 counts.
  5. Repeat 2 to 4 times, then return to normal breathing.

One round adds up to 11 to 14 counts. At a count a second, two rounds take about 30 seconds and four take about a minute. The workbook allows one to two minutes for the whole practice, which leaves room to settle in first and to take a few ordinary breaths afterward.

The counts are a guide. Maya Chen teaches this same sigh with a 4-count breath in and up to three rounds, next to a slower practice, in two breathing exercises to calm down when you're stressed. If 4 suits you better than 3, use 4. The part to keep is a breath out that lasts longer than the breath in.

If the double inhale feels uncomfortable, try a single deep breath in for 4 counts and a long breath out for 8. If you need to be silent, breathe out through your nose. People in the Stanford trial were allowed to do the whole sigh through the nose (Balban et al., 2023).

On this page the sigh stands alone. In the Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook it is the first of four tools in Chapter 3: humming and cold water, a practice for looping thoughts and muscle relaxation follow it, with a page where you assign each tool to the moments that set you off.

What you might notice

  • A big yawn or an involuntary sigh. Common, and worth letting through unless you're mid-presentation.
  • Warmth in your chest or shoulders. Some women feel this as they slow down.
  • Feeling light-headed for a breath. It can happen after the first round and usually passes quickly. If it doesn't, stop and breathe normally.
  • Nothing. Also normal. Regulation is often quiet at first.

A quiet first try doesn't mean you did it wrong. In the Stanford trial, the lift in mood grew with the number of days people practiced (Balban et al., 2023), so one flat round on a hard Tuesday tells you very little.

Regulation is often quiet at first.

And if the sigh leaves you more wound up than before, drop it for today. Some days breath is the wrong door. Look around the room, feel your feet on the floor, and try again another time or leave it alone.

When to use it: the meeting, the car, 3 a.m.

In a meeting. Keep your eyes on the screen and breathe out through your nose so it stays silent. Two rounds fit comfortably inside someone else's status update.

In the car. Before you turn the key, or stopped at a red light, with your eyes open. If you're driving and feel at all light-headed, breathe normally and pull over when you safely can.

At 3 a.m. It works lying down, in the dark, without waking anyone. Do 2 to 4 rounds, then let your breathing go back to normal. It may not send you back to sleep, but it gives you something to do other than negotiate with the ceiling. If that wake-up is a regular visitor, why 3 a.m. anxiety isn't in your head looks at what may be going on.

And if the meeting is also where a word you use every week goes missing, that has its own post: perimenopause brain fog, what it is and what it is not.

It also helps to practice once when nothing is wrong. Pick one predictable moment this week, like the mid-afternoon slump. Before you reach for your phone or another coffee, do two rounds, about 30 seconds. Then notice what your body does. No transformation required.

Questions women ask about the physiological sigh

How do you do the physiological sigh? Breathe in through your nose, add a small sniff on top without breathing out, then let one long, slow breath out. The workbook counts 3 for the breath in, about one second for the sniff and 6 to 8 for the breath out. Repeat 2 to 4 times, then return to normal breathing.

How long does the physiological sigh take? At a count a second, two rounds take about 30 seconds and four take about a minute. A quiet first try doesn't mean you did it wrong: in the Stanford trial, the lift in mood grew with the number of days people practiced (Balban et al., 2023).

Does the physiological sigh help with anxiety? It may. In a small trial its authors describe as exploratory, every group felt less anxious after a session, with no clear winner on anxiety between the breathing exercises and the meditation (Balban et al., 2023). The people in it were mostly students practicing five minutes a day, so it says nothing specific about perimenopause.

The sigh is Tool 1 in Chapter 3 of the Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook, where it sits beside three other short tools and a planner for matching each one to the moments that set you off.
source: The Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook, Chapter 3: The 10-Minute Calm Toolkit (Tool 1: The Physiological Sigh)

author: claire-harmon
title: Menopause Brain Fog: How to Map When It Shows Up
dek: Menopause brain fog can feel random. A 14-day notebook map, about 90 seconds a morning, shows when it comes and what it travels with.
seo_title: Menopause Brain Fog: How to Map When It Shows Up
seo_description: Menopause brain fog, mapped: a 14-day notebook log of clarity, sleep, night sweats and stress, and how to read it before a doctor's visit.
pull_quote: A rough map with honest numbers beats a perfect log you abandoned on day four.
body_html:
It's 2:40 on a Wednesday afternoon. You have read the same email three times, and the name of the colleague you're answering has left the building. Yesterday you were sharp. Tomorrow could go either way.

That is the maddening part of menopause brain fog. It seems to keep no schedule: a good Tuesday, a useless Wednesday, a fine Thursday. Random is hard to live with, because you can't plan around it and you can't explain it to anyone.

It may be less random than it looks. This entry gives you one small practice, a two-week map of when the fog shows up, how strong it is and what it travels with. You need a notebook, a pen and about 90 seconds a day.

Why menopause brain fog is worth mapping

I've written separately about what perimenopause brain fog is and what it isn't, so I won't repeat it here. For the map, one finding matters. A review written for the International Menopause Society names hot flashes, disturbed sleep and mood among the things that influence thinking at midlife (Maki & Jaff, 2022).

A review describes groups of women. It can't say which of those things, if any, is tangled up with your foggy Wednesdays. A map shows patterns. It doesn't diagnose anything, and it can't settle what causes what. What it can do is turn "I keep forgetting things" into a page you can look at.

When to talk to your doctor first

Some changes shouldn't wait for two weeks of notes. Contact your doctor promptly, or seek urgent care, if a change is sudden or getting worse quickly. Talk to your doctor soon if you are getting lost in places you know well or having trouble with everyday tasks you used to do without thinking. Brain fog can have more than one explanation, and a doctor is the person who can sort through them with you. The map below is meant to support professional care, and it does not replace it.

Set up your 14-day fog map

Open a notebook and rule six columns and fourteen rows, one row per day. Head the columns Clarity, Sleep, Night sweats, Stress, Cycle day and Lapses. Leave a margin for one or two words about the day, such as "deadline" or "good sleep." It is the closest thing to a brain fog tracker you can make with a ruler.

The last column uses four letters, shorthand for the common shapes of fog:

  • W for a lost word: a name or a word you know well, gone mid-sentence.
  • D for the empty doorway: arriving somewhere with no idea why you came.
  • A for divided attention: two things at once is suddenly one too many.
  • T for mental tiredness: thinking feels slower and heavier.

The morning check-in, step by step

Do this once a day for 14 days, before you pick up your phone. It takes about 90 seconds.

  1. Close your eyes for five seconds. Find one honest word for how your head feels this morning.
  2. Write your clarity number, 0 to 10. 0 is "I can barely form a sentence." 10 is "sharp and focused." Most days land in the middle. The first number that comes to mind wins.
  3. Note last night. Write roughly how many hours you slept, whether the sleep was broken, and yes or no for night sweats or hot flashes overnight.
  4. Write your stress number, 0 to 10. It stands for how much pressure you are carrying.
  5. Add your cycle day, if you still track it. Otherwise write "irregular" or leave it blank.
  6. Record yesterday's lapses. Write W, D, A or T, whichever applied. One letter, two or none.

A finished row might read: clarity 3, five hours, broken, night sweats yes, stress 6, irregular, W and T. No sentences required.

On a day when even that is too much, write only the clarity number. One number keeps the map going. And try not to analyze as you go. The reading comes after day 14.

You will miss a day at some point. Leave the row empty and pick up at the next one. Nothing resets, and there is no perfect run to protect. An empty row tells you something too: if the gaps bunch together, look at what was happening that week, because the gap can be part of the pattern. A rough map with honest numbers beats a perfect log you abandoned on day four.

A rough map with honest numbers beats a perfect log you abandoned on day four.

How to read your map after day 14

Set aside about 10 minutes. You are looking for a cluster, meaning low clarity that tends to show up alongside something else.

  1. Circle your lowest days. Mark every day with a clarity score of 4 or below.
  2. Look at what came before. For each circled day, check the night before and the day before for broken sleep, night sweats, stress of 7 or more, or a certain point in your cycle.
  3. Look for the repeat. See whether the same thing shows up before most of your low days. It doesn't have to be every time.
  4. Notice your best days too. Write down what your clearest days have in common. Good days are as informative as hard ones.

Then count which lapse letter showed up most, and whether it keeps company with anything in the other columns.

This map is the Morning Check-In, Tool 02a in Chapter 2 of The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook. The paperback prints the 14-day log as two weekly pages, plus a four-week fog calendar to shade. The chapter ends with a guided pattern reading, and other chapters cover what else can cause fog, paper backups, the fog multipliers (sleep, night sweats and stress) and your doctor's visit.

What you might notice

Picture Renée, 51, an accountant who works from home. She is a composite of many women, and she was sure her fog was random. By day ten her page said otherwise: her worst days almost always followed the nights she woke up drenched.

Other maps look different. One woman's hardest days may line up with her highest stress scores and have little to do with sleep. Another may need both at once, broken sleep plus a heavy workload, before the fog gets bad. No pattern is the "right" one.

You might also find no pattern at all. That is information too. It may mean you need a longer window, and it never means you did it wrong.

If the map makes you more anxious, drop back to the one clarity number, or put it away. If something you notice feels sudden, very different or frightening, stop and call your doctor.

When to use it

  • When the fog feels random and you have started to dread it.
  • In the two weeks before a doctor's visit, so you arrive with a page of notes.
  • For another two weeks later on, if the first map showed nothing obvious or your days have changed.

What to do with your fog map

The map has three jobs. The first is knowing what a foggy day is about. A low score after a night of hot-flash wake-ups can become this may be what last night cost me, which is easier to carry than what is wrong with my brain? If your map keeps pointing at the nights, and the nights include lying awake with a racing heart, I've written about 3 a.m. anxiety in perimenopause as well.

The second job is choosing one thing to work on, and leaving the rest alone for now. The map can suggest which one is most likely to matter for you.

The third is the doctor's visit. Bring the notebook. You could say: "I've tracked my brain fog for two weeks and I see a pattern around sleep and night sweats. Can we talk about that, and about whether anything else should be checked?"

When your map is ready, here is how to talk to your doctor about brain fog, with a one-page summary to bring.

Questions women ask about tracking menopause brain fog

How do I track menopause brain fog? One row a day in a notebook for 14 days: a clarity number from 0 to 10, last night's sleep, night sweats, a stress number, your cycle day and yesterday's lapses. It takes about 90 seconds each morning, before you pick up your phone. On a hard day, the clarity number alone keeps the map going.

Why is menopause brain fog worse on some days than others? No blog post can tell you that about yours. A review written for the International Menopause Society names hot flashes, disturbed sleep and mood among the things that influence thinking at midlife (Maki & Jaff, 2022). A two-week map can show what your low days tend to follow, though it shows patterns and can't settle what causes what.

What should I tell my doctor about brain fog? Bring the notebook, say what you tracked and what pattern you see, and ask whether anything else should be checked. Don't wait for two weeks of notes if a change is sudden or getting worse quickly, or if everyday tasks have become hard. Brain fog can have more than one explanation, and a doctor is the person who can sort through them with you.

The full map, with its log pages printed in the paperback, is in The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook. If your low days keep pointing at stress that feels more like anxiety than workload, my Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook is a separate book for that. For today, a notebook and tomorrow morning's first number are enough to begin.
source: The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook, Chapter 2 (Tool 02a, The Morning Check-In, and the 14-Day Clarity and Symptom Log)

author: claire-harmon
title: Perimenopause Brain Fog: What It Is and What It Is Not
dek: What perimenopause brain fog tends to look like, what it is not, when to talk to a doctor, and a seven-day pen-and-paper practice to start today.
seo_title: Perimenopause Brain Fog: What It Is and What It Is Not
seo_description: Perimenopause brain fog: lost words, empty doorways, what it is not, when to talk to a doctor, and a seven-day Lapse List you can start today.
pull_quote: One week of watching can tell you more than months of worrying.
body_html:
You are standing in the laundry room holding a spoon. You have no idea why.

Somewhere between the kitchen counter and here, the reason fell out of your head. You retrace your steps. Kitchen. Hallway. Laundry room. Nothing. Earlier, in a meeting, a word you use every week was simply gone. You said the thing and hoped nobody noticed. Nobody did. You did.

This is what perimenopause brain fog tends to look like: small, ordinary, and frightening out of all proportion to its size. Here is what it is, what it is not, and one pen-and-paper practice you can start today.

What perimenopause brain fog tends to look like

It rarely looks dramatic, which is part of why it unsettles. A white paper of the International Menopause Society lists the usual complaints: trouble recalling words and numbers, everyday slips such as misplacing keys, losing your train of thought, being more easily distracted, and forgetting appointments. Together they are often called brain fog (Maki & Jaff, 2022). You will also see it called menopause brain fog, although the same paper places the start of these difficulties in perimenopause, when cycles become irregular.

It can help to sort the fog into four shapes:

  • Lost words. A name or a word you know well, gone mid-sentence.
  • The empty doorway. Arriving somewhere with no idea why you came.
  • Divided attention. Two things at once is suddenly one too many.
  • Mental tiredness. Thinking feels slower and heavier, like working through static.

Picture Lena, 49, two months into a new job. She is a composite, drawn from many common experiences. In meetings, a colleague's name sometimes goes blank, and the embarrassment follows her around all day. You may have one shape or all four, and they can shift from week to week.

Why it is so frightening

A lost word is a small thing. What it seems to point toward is large, and many women carry that thought alone. The search tends to happen at midnight, which is why 3 a.m. anxiety in perimenopause has its own post.

Fear can also make it harder to think clearly, and then the next lapse feeds the fear. In one study of perimenopausal women, memory complaints went along with anxiety, depressive symptoms and disturbed sleep. They were tied to attention and working memory, and showed no link to verbal memory itself (Weber et al., 2012). That is an association in one group of women, and it cannot say which came first.

What may be going on

No blog post can tell you what is behind your fog. Here is what researchers describe in groups of women. The change seen most reliably during the transition is in learning and verbal memory. Planning and strategic thinking do not change in long-term studies. How much a woman is affected varies widely, it is nearly always mild, and average performance stays within normal limits (Maki & Jaff, 2022).

The same paper says that falling estradiol, hot flashes, disturbed sleep and mood all influence thinking at midlife. So the fog may have more than one contributor, and hormones are one possible explanation among several. On how long it lasts, the authors conclude that memory difficulties resolve in many women and persist in some.

What brain fog is not

It is no character flaw, and it is no measure of how hard you are trying.

The fear underneath usually has a name: dementia. The white paper states that the thinking changes of menopause should not be confused with dementia, and that dementia before age 64 is rare (Maki & Jaff, 2022). A guide for health professionals describes the difference this way (British Menopause Society, 2026). Brain fog is noticed mostly by the woman herself, can fluctuate, does not affect independent living and usually improves after menopause. Dementia is progressive, is noticed by other people, affects independence and is more common after 65.

Those are descriptions of patterns in groups of women. They cannot tell you which one you are living in, and neither can I. A doctor can. The same guide notes that brain fog is not always hormonal, and it lists other illnesses, nutritional deficiencies, mental health conditions, life circumstances, sleep and medication among the things to check.

When to talk to a doctor

None of these tells you what is going on. Each one is a reason to book an appointment soon, and a sudden change, or one that is getting worse quickly, is a reason to contact your doctor promptly or seek urgent care:

  • A sudden change in your memory or thinking, or one that is getting worse quickly.
  • Losing your way somewhere you know well. Whatever the reason turns out to be, it is worth having looked at.
  • Trouble with everyday tasks you normally manage on your own.
  • Someone close to you mentioning a change. It says nothing about the cause, and it is useful to bring to the visit.
  • A worry that will not settle, whatever any list says.

That last one counts. Being worried is a legitimate reason to be checked. The practice below is meant to support professional care, and it does not replace it.

A practice for today: the Lapse List

Brain fog is slippery. When a doctor asks how often it happens, you honestly don't know. The Lapse List puts it on paper. Using something physical to take load off your memory has a name, cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016), which is a grand title for the back of an envelope. This week you are only watching the fog. One week of watching can tell you more than months of worrying.

One week of watching can tell you more than months of worrying.

Safety note: if writing about your lapses makes you more anxious, keep entries to three words or fewer. This is a noticing tool. You can stop at any time.

Setup: keep the list where you can reach it within 30 seconds. A small notebook, a sticky note on your desk or the back of an envelope all work. Run it for seven days. Each entry takes a few seconds.

  1. Write 3 to 5 words. Do it within a minute or two of the lapse: "Lost name in meeting." "Keys in fridge." Speed beats detail.
  2. Add what you did next. "Paused, it came back." "Retraced steps." "Asked a colleague." This is noticing that you recovered.
  3. Add a context if you notice one. Tired, bad night, stressful morning. If nothing stands out, leave it blank. Never force a reason.
  4. Glance at the list at the end of each day. No analysis. Close it and move on.
  5. Read the whole list after seven days. See whether lapses cluster at a time of day, after a kind of night or in certain situations. Write down what you notice.

If seven days feels like too much, start with three. If the list gets long, keep only the two or three biggest lapses of the day.

The Lapse List is Tool 01a in Chapter 1 of The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook. The paperback prints a seven-day Lapse List log to fill in, and the chapter adds the Lapse Tally for tired days. Later chapters turn the list into a 14-day map (Chapter 2), build paper backups for your memory (Chapter 4) and a one-page summary for your doctor (Chapter 7).

What you might notice

Relief, because written down it often feels smaller than it did in your head. Surprise: there may be fewer lapses than you feared, or they may cluster in ways you did not expect. A flicker of shame, which is common.

You might also notice nothing: no pattern, and no feeling either way. That is information too. If the list starts to feed the worry, shorten the entries, drop to three days or put it away.

When to use it

  • The week before a doctor's appointment. "I lost words in conversations four times this week, mostly in the afternoon" gives a doctor far more to work with than "I've been forgetting things."
  • When the worry is loudest. A short list can be easier to look at than a feeling.
  • After a run of bad nights, to see whether the fog follows them.

For the day to day, these brain fog memory tips put a few paper backups in place.

Questions women ask about perimenopause brain fog

What does perimenopause brain fog feel like? Mostly small and ordinary: a word you know well gone mid-sentence, arriving in a room with no idea why you came, two things at once suddenly being one too many, thinking that feels slower and heavier. You may have one of these or all four, and they can shift from week to week.

How long does perimenopause brain fog last? It varies, and no one can give you a date. The authors of the International Menopause Society white paper conclude that memory difficulties resolve in many women and persist in some (Maki & Jaff, 2022). For your own fog, a doctor is the person to ask.

When should I see a doctor about brain fog? Contact your doctor promptly, or seek urgent care, if a change in your memory or thinking is sudden or getting worse quickly. Book an appointment soon if you have trouble with everyday tasks you normally manage on your own. A worry that will not settle is also a legitimate reason to be checked. Brain fog is not always hormonal, and a doctor can look at the other things worth checking (British Menopause Society, 2026).

Worry about memory and anxiety can feed each other, and a lost word is harder to wait for when your heart is racing. When the worry comes on fast, the physiological sigh takes a minute or two. The rest of the method for the fog is in The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook. If the anxiety is the louder part, my Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook is a separate book for that. For today, an envelope and a pen are enough to begin.

title: Brain Fog Memory Tips: Paper Backups for Foggy Days
dek: Brain fog memory tips that carry the load for you: seven paper backups and a 10-minute landing spot you can set up today.
seo_title: Brain Fog Memory Tips: Paper Backups for Foggy Days
seo_description: Brain fog memory tips on paper: a landing spot, a word bank, a one-page meeting note, a plan B, and one backup to set up in 10 minutes today.
pull_quote: The goal is not to try harder. It is to carry less.
body_html:
It's 8:10 on a Tuesday and you are standing in the hallway with your coat on, patting every pocket. The keys were in your hand five minutes ago. You find them in the bathroom, next to the toothpaste, with no memory of putting them there.

If you have been searching for brain fog memory tips, here is the short answer. The tips that tend to hold up on a foggy day are not about remembering harder. They are about carrying less: moving what your memory keeps dropping onto paper, in one fixed place, tied to something you already do every day. Below are seven paper backups, and one you can set up today in about 10 minutes.

Why paper backups can help a foggy memory

I've written separately about what perimenopause brain fog is and what it is not, so this entry stays practical.

Using something physical to lower the load on your memory has a name: cognitive offloading. Risko and Gilbert describe it as using a physical action to change what a task demands of you and reduce the mental load, like setting your phone to remind you of an appointment (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). Writing something down is offloading. So is keeping your keys in the same spot every day.

None of this makes you less capable. Picture Joanne, 49, in the first week of a new job. She is a composite, like the other women here. By Tuesday she had lost her glasses four times before lunch. By Friday she had stopped blaming herself and picked one spot for them: the left corner of her desk, next to the monitor. Within a week she was hardly searching at all. Not because her brain had changed. She had stopped asking it to remember something it was no longer reliably doing.

Brain fog memory tips: seven paper backups

One rule runs through all seven. Each backup lives on paper, in one fixed place, and is attached to something you already do. If a system needs a good brain day to keep going, it won't survive a bad one.

  • A landing spot. One fixed place for the thing you lose most: keys, glasses, badge or phone. Not a drawer, and not "somewhere on the counter." One visible spot your hands learn to go to without your brain deciding.
  • A word bank. A small running list, on an index card or the inside cover of a notebook, of the words that disappear on you most: colleagues' names, work terms, phrases you need in meetings. Add one detail to place each person ("Marcus, IT, sits near the window"). Read it two minutes before a meeting. Not during.
  • A one-page meeting note. Four parts, for any conversation that matters, whether it's a meeting, a hard phone call or a medical appointment: what I need to cover, what I heard, what I'm doing next (one step, with a day), and what I still want to ask.
  • The "before" line. Of those four parts, the first matters most. Write the two or three things you must not leave without before the conversation starts. Once they are on paper, you can listen instead of trying to remember.
  • An anchor. BJ Fogg's recipe for tiny habits is "After I [something I already do], I will [new tiny behavior]," where the anchor is a moment that already happens reliably every day (Fogg, 2020).
  • A plan B, decided in advance. An "if... then I will..." plan is decided while you're calm, so you don't decide again in a foggy moment. Research on these plans, called implementation intentions, links them to following through on goals (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006), and later work suggests the effect is more modest than first thought.
  • An end-of-week check. On Sunday, mark the days you used each backup, then decide: keep it, tweak it or drop it. Dropping one is allowed.

You don't need all seven. Start with the one that fixes what you lose most.

A practice for today: your first landing spot

You need a pen, a sticky note and a calm moment. It takes about 10 minutes.

A note before you start: if this begins to feel like a list of everything you can no longer do, stop. One plan is enough to begin.

  1. Pick the one thing you lose most often. Just one to start: keys, glasses, phone or badge.
  2. Pick a visible surface you pass every day. Close to the door you use most, and not inside a bag.
  3. Mark it if that helps. A small tray, a hook or one corner of a shelf.
  4. Write your anchor. "After I ____, I will put ____ in ____." For example: after I close the front door, I will put my keys on the hook. The moment the door closes, not "in a minute."
  5. Write your plan B. "If I can't do that, then I will ____." For example: if my hands are full, my keys go in my left coat pocket, always the left, and move to the hook as soon as the bags are down.
  6. Put it where the moment happens. Copy the anchor and the plan B onto a sticky note and stick it beside the spot.
  7. Check at the end of the week. Mark the days you used it, then keep, tweak or drop it. Add a second thing only when the first one runs without thinking.

After a few weeks of the same motion at the door, your hands may know what to do before your brain does. That's the aim: a system that runs on a foggy day without a decision. The goal is not to try harder. It is to carry less.

The goal is not to try harder. It is to carry less.

These backups come from Chapter 4, "Your Outside Brain," of The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook. There each one gets an If... Then I Will... plan, and the paperback prints a word bank, a landing-spots table, meeting-note pages and an end-of-week check. When the hardest part is what a lost word seems to mean, Chapter 3 has A Jar for the Fear and a Check the Facts page.

What you might notice

  • Awkwardness. That is what a habit tends to feel like before it is automatic.
  • "I never needed this before." Your brain did this work out of sight. Right now it may be carrying more.
  • A little less dread. Picture Anita, a nurse who uses a meeting note for shift handoffs. After two weeks she felt less anxious going into them. Not because she remembered more. Because she trusted the important things were written down.
  • Nothing much, for a while. That's common too. A slow start doesn't mean you did it wrong.

If setting it up leaves you feeling worse, put the rest away and keep only the plan B.

When to use it

  • In a week full of new information: a new job, a move, a heavy deadline.
  • Before the calls where a lost word costs you most. Add the word bank: before your first call, take 20 seconds to read the card and write one thing you need to cover.
  • On a foggy day, when the plan B is the plan.

How to cope with brain fog when the system slips

Every system fails some days. The word card is in your other coat. You skip the meeting note for two weeks during a deadline. Missing time resets nothing. Pick it up again the next Monday. The system is still there.

No list of perimenopause brain fog tips can tell you what is behind your fog. If you want to see when it shows up and what travels with it, I've written about how to map when menopause brain fog shows up with a 14-day notebook log. The backups carry the load; the map shows the pattern.

One calm note on when not to wait. Contact your doctor promptly, or seek urgent care, if a change in your memory or thinking is sudden or getting worse quickly. Talk to your doctor soon if everyday tasks have become hard to manage. Needing reminders for things you used to hold easily is worth mentioning too. These backups are meant to support professional care, and they do not replace it.

Questions women ask about brain fog memory tips

What are the most useful brain fog memory tips for work? At work, three tend to do the most: a word bank you read two minutes before a meeting, a one-page meeting note with what you need to cover written before it starts, and one fixed spot for your badge or glasses.

Is it cheating to write everything down? No. Using paper or a reminder to lower the load on your memory is a recognized strategy called cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016). Once the important things are on paper, you can listen instead of trying to hold everything at once.

What if I forget to use the system? Plan for that in advance. Write an "if... then I will..." plan B for each backup and put it on a sticky note where the moment happens. Missing a day resets nothing, so pick it up again at the next anchor.

The backups, with pages to fill in, are in The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook. For today, a sticky note and one spot by the door are enough to begin.

seo_title: How to Talk to Your Doctor About Brain Fog in Perimenopause
seo_description: Talk to your doctor about brain fog with one page: what to write before, what to say during and what to note after your perimenopause appointment.
pull_quote: You are not asking for a favor. You are describing something new that is affecting your life.
body_html:
Marisol, 48, rehearsed in the car. She had it ready: the client's name that went blank mid-meeting, the paragraph she read four times. Then the doctor sat down, glanced at the screen, and Marisol heard herself say, "It's probably nothing. I'm just tired." Ten minutes later she was back in the parking lot with nothing written down. (Marisol is a composite, drawn from many women's experiences.)

If you want to talk to your doctor about brain fog and you're afraid the same thing will happen, here is the short version. Your job is not to convince anyone. It is to describe what is new, when it started and how it affects your days, and to bring that on one page. This entry walks you through before, during and after the appointment, with a one-page summary you can write today.

Why it is hard to talk to your doctor about brain fog

Most of us minimize before we begin. We hand the doctor an easy exit ("it's probably stress") before we have said what we came to say.

Then there is the fog itself. A white paper of the International Menopause Society lists trouble recalling words among the usual complaints, along with losing your train of thought and forgetting appointments (Maki & Jaff, 2022). So the very thing you came to describe can get in the way of describing it, in a small room, with the clock running. That is why most of the work is best done before you walk in. You are not asking for a favor. You are describing something new that is affecting your life.

You are not asking for a favor. You are describing something new that is affecting your life.

If you are still working out whether this is brain fog at all, start with what perimenopause brain fog is and what it is not.

When not to wait for a routine appointment

Some changes should not wait for a page of notes. Contact your doctor promptly, or seek urgent care, if a change in your memory or thinking is sudden or getting worse quickly, if you are getting lost in places you know well, or if your safety is affected. Brain fog can have more than one explanation, and a doctor is the person who can sort through them with you. Everything below is meant to support professional care, and it does not replace it.

Before: write a one-page appointment summary

Appointments are short, and one tidy page is easier to act on than a long explanation under pressure. Write it in the words you would use with a friend. You don't need to sound medical. You need to sound specific.

How long: about 15 minutes to write, plus about 5 minutes to read it aloud the day before. What you need: a sheet of paper, a pen and any notes you have kept, such as a 14-day menopause brain fog map. If you have the map, bring it to the appointment too.

A gentle note: if writing this down stirs up fear, keep each line short. You can stop at any point and come back to it tomorrow.

  1. Write what is new and when it started. One or two lines. For example: "This level of forgetting is new for me. It started about six months ago."
  2. Add two or three concrete examples. Choose the ones that happen most often: a lost word in a meeting, reading the same paragraph three times, walking into a room with no idea why.
  3. Note what it seems to travel with. From your map, if you kept one: poor sleep, night sweats, changes in your cycle, stressful weeks. If you have no notes, write what you have noticed. "Not sure" is an honest answer.
  4. Write how it affects your daily life. Work, relationships, confidence. This is often the sentence that gets heard. For example: "It is affecting my work. I'm struggling to follow conversations."
  5. List the medicines and supplements you take. Names are enough. It saves you from trying to remember them in the room.
  6. Write up to three questions. Written down, not memorized. Put the one you most need answered first.
  7. Read the page out loud once, the day before. Notice which line was hardest to say. That is probably the most important one, so underline it.

What to bring: the page (one copy to hand over and one to read from), your map or notebook, a pen and, if it helps, someone you trust to take notes.

What you might notice: relief, because on paper it often looks smaller than it felt in your head. Tears when you read it aloud, which are common. A feeling that the page looks thin; specific beats long. Or nothing much at all, which is fine too. If the page starts to feed the worry, put it down and finish it tomorrow.

When to use it: the week before an appointment; the night before, for one quiet read; and before any follow-up visit, with the new questions at the top.

This summary comes from Chapter 7 of The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook, "Talk to Your Doctor About Brain Fog" (Exercise 07b). The chapter adds a timeline of when it started, a practice run out loud, phrases for when you feel dismissed and an after-visit review. The paperback prints the summary as a page to take with you, plus a one-line-per-visit appointment log.

During: what to tell your doctor about brain fog

Start by reading your first line, word for word. Reading from a page is not a weakness. It is preparation. Here are some example phrasings that keep the conversation specific; use your own words if they fit better:

  • "This is new for me. I don't normally forget like this."
  • "It is affecting my work."
  • "I tracked it for two weeks, and I'd like to show you what I found."
  • "My worst days seem to follow my worst nights."
  • "I'm frightened this means something worse, and I'd like to talk about that."

That fourth line is worth saying if your notes show it. The International Menopause Society white paper names hot flashes, disturbed sleep and mood among the things that influence thinking at midlife (Maki & Jaff, 2022). Your doctor can help you work out what a pattern means for you.

Some example questions, to choose from for your page:

  • "Could this be related to perimenopause?"
  • "What else would you want to rule out?"
  • "Are there sleep or mood factors we should look at alongside this?"
  • "If we try something, how will we know whether it's helping?"

The second question is a fair one. A guide written for health professionals notes that brain fog is not always hormonal, and it lists other illnesses, sleep and medication among the things to consider (British Menopause Society, 2026). Asking does not mean something else is going on. It means you have both looked.

If you hear "it's probably just stress," you might say, for example: "I understand. I'd still like to make sure we've considered other possibilities. Can we look at this together?" That is not confrontation. It is advocacy.

Before you leave, ask: "Can you tell me in one sentence what we decided today and what happens next?" Write the answer down, or ask them to.

After the perimenopause doctor appointment: a five-minute review

You will remember things in the car and may forget exactly what comes next. So write a short review within 24 hours. Four lines are enough:

  1. What I heard: in plain words, what the doctor said might be happening.
  2. What we decided: the next step, whether that is a follow-up, a referral or waiting and watching.
  3. What I still need to ask: the question from the drive home. It becomes the first line of your next summary.
  4. How I feel about it: relieved, worried, frustrated. Honest, not polished.

If the appointment left you feeling unheard, write that down too: "I didn't feel heard about the lost words. I still want to ask about sleep." It is information for the next conversation, with the same doctor or a different one. Let's Talk Menopause, a US nonprofit, has a finder for menopause specialists on its website.

Questions women ask about talking to your doctor about brain fog

What should I tell my doctor about brain fog? Say what is new, when it started, two or three concrete examples and how it affects your daily life. If you have kept notes, say what you tracked and what pattern you see. One written page makes this much easier to do in a short appointment.

What if my doctor says it's just stress? You can stay calm and specific: "I understand. I'd still like to make sure we've considered other possibilities." Brain fog can have more than one explanation, so asking what else to rule out is a reasonable request. If you still leave feeling unheard, write down what was missed and take it to the next appointment.

Is it okay to read from notes at the appointment? Yes. Reading from a page is preparation, not weakness, and with brain fog in the room it may be the most reliable way to say what you came to say. You can hand over one copy and read from the other.

The summary page, the after-visit review and the fog map they draw on are in The Perimenopause Brain Fog Workbook. If anxiety is part of what you want to raise, my Perimenopause Anxiety Workbook has its own chapter on this appointment. For today, a sheet of paper and the first line are enough to begin.
